title: The EU's next seven-year budget
deck: Leaders want to agree the 2028-2034 EU budget by the end of 2026, but an Austrian veto threat, a Parliament defending its programmes and a French election that could rewrite Paris's position all pull against a quick deal.
region: Brussels, European Union (France, Germany, Poland, Spain, Italy, Austria)

fuel.title: Austria threatens veto on budget
fuel.how: The budget needs unanimity among member states, so one government's veto threat can stall or reshape the whole package.

fuel.title: Parliament shields Erasmus and research
fuel.how: Spending demands from Parliament and lobbies collide with rising debt repayment bills, which squeezes the room for a deal.

fuel.title: Ukraine funding depends on next budget
fuel.how: Much of the aid for Kyiv flows through EU channels, so the size of the budget sets Europe's capacity to fund Ukraine after 2027.

fuel.title: Green Deal rules need budget money
fuel.how: Enforcement of the deforestation and carbon border rules is funded from the EU budget, which Le Pen has promised to stop.

card.headline: Europe wants its next seven-year budget agreed before voters in France, Spain, Italy and Poland can change the maths

forYou.line: The deforestation rules apply from 30 December 2026 and carbon border certificates go on sale 1 February 2027. Enforcement money sits in the budget fight.
Parliament is pushing to protect Erasmus and research funding as debt repayment bills mount.
Dozens of European organisations are lobbying to keep transport funding in the 2028-2034 budget.
A single veto, such as the one Austria is reported to be weighing, can stall the whole package. Treat a year-end deal as possible, not likely.
The budget decides how much Europe can spend on Ukraine, climate rules and shared projects after 2027, and the French vote could change France's stance.

effects.text: Austria threatens to block approval of the 2028-2034 budget; Chancellor Stocker is reported to be considering a veto
Parliament moves to protect Erasmus and research funding while debt repayment bills mount
Dozens of European organisations demand transport funding be maintained
Macron presses leaders for a deal this year, before the French vote
Every government and lobby group now bids for its own line, which makes a clean deal by 31 December harder
Uncertainty over EU funding capacity after 2027 clouds planning for Ukraine support
Importers and regulators face the deforestation and carbon border rules with the budget that funds enforcement still unsettled
If no deal lands before the 2027 votes, new governments in France, Spain, Italy and Poland can reopen positions
A French win for the National Rally would put a cap on France's contribution, Ukraine aid and Green Deal funding on the table
A long delay could push the EU toward stopgap annual budgeting after the current framework ends in 2027

whatHappened: EU leaders are trying to agree the bloc's next seven-year budget, covering 2028 to 2034, by the end of 2026. The aim is to settle it before elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland can change who sits at the table.

On 26 October, reports said Austria was threatening to block approval and that Chancellor Stocker was considering a veto. The budget needs unanimity in the Council, so a single government can hold it up.

In the same days, the European Parliament moved to protect Erasmus and research funding as debt repayment bills mount. Dozens of European organisations called for transport funding to be kept. A headline on 25 October said Council President Costa had set the next budget showdown, but we do not have the details.

France is the central political thread. Macron told EU leaders Paris wants a deal this year. The National Rally candidate leads October polls at 35-36%. Marine Le Pen wants France's net contribution cut from about EUR 8bn to EUR 5bn and calls the rush anti-democratic.
whyItMatters: Politics: the budget needs every member state to agree, and then Parliament's consent. Austria's veto threat shows how one government can stall a package worth about EUR 2 trillion (the Commission's July 2025 proposal, from our general knowledge). The calendar adds pressure. France votes on 18 April and 2 May 2027, Spain is heading to a snap election, and Le Pen has named Spain among the elections she says the Commission is racing.

Public money: the budget is a fight over limited room. Parliament wants Erasmus and research protected, transport groups want their line kept, and debt repayment bills are rising. A new Competitiveness Fund is also reshaping the logic of what the budget is for, according to Elcano's analysis. Every extra demand makes a quick deal harder.

Security: much of the aid that goes to Ukraine comes through EU channels, not single countries. If a ceasefire or deal changes Kyiv's needs, the size and flexibility of the next budget set Europe's capacity to respond after 2027. Le Pen pledges to end Ukraine funding within six months.

Trade and the Green Deal: the deforestation regulation applies to large and medium operators from 30 December 2026 and to small firms from 30 June 2027. Carbon border certificates go on sale on 1 February 2027. The next budget funds enforcement, and Le Pen has promised to stop the Green Deal, so importers and regulators depend on the same political fight.

winners.who: Governments that hold a veto and use it
winners.why: Austria's threat gives Vienna leverage over spending lines, national rebates or the overall size. We do not know what Vienna wants, so this is a general point.

winners.who: Macron's camp, if a deal lands in 2026
winners.why: A deal agreed before the vote locks in a larger-budget position that a new French government would find harder to unwind.
Parliament, the transport groups and research bodies are early with demands, and well-defended programmes tend to survive the cuts.
The rush to a deal feeds its claim that Brussels is racing the voters, and the budget becomes a campaign issue.

losers.why: Any delay or cut to the budget narrows the EU channel for funding Kyiv after 2027, and Zelensky has already answered Le Pen's pledge to cut French aid.
With debt bills rising and many bidders, the lines that lack a defender are the likeliest to be trimmed.
They face the new deforestation and carbon border rules while the money behind enforcement is still uncertain.
A slipping deadline leaves regions, universities and infrastructure builders without a firm number for 2028 onward.

whatsNext: Late 2026: leaders aim to settle the budget. A year-end deal is the stated goal, but one veto, or a threat of one, can push talks into 2027.
30 December 2026: the deforestation rules start for large and medium operators. The first test of enforcement lands before the budget is settled.
1 February 2027: carbon border certificate sales open.
Spring 2027: France votes on 18 April and 2 May. Spain's snap election date is not yet confirmed.
The current seven-year framework ends on 31 December 2027, so the real hard stop is the end of next year, not this one.

predict.question: Before you read the scenarios: what do you think is the most likely outcome for the budget?
options: Leaders agree a full deal before the end of 2026
Talks slip into 2027, with a deal only after the French vote is in view
Austria's veto stalls talks well into 2028
A new French government rewrites the deal after the election
predict.explanation: Our base case, at about 45%, is that talks slip into 2027. Past EU budgets took long to settle, and a veto threat, a protective Parliament and many competing lobbies make a deal by 31 December unlikely. A year-end deal is our second most likely path at about 25%.

timeline.title: Commission proposes the 2028-2034 budget
timeline.detail: The proposal was for roughly EUR 2 trillion over seven years, including a new competitiveness fund and a reserve for Ukraine. This is from general knowledge and not from the listed sources; details are approximate.

timeline.title: Euronews examines what a Le Pen win would mean
timeline.detail: The piece sets out her pledges to end Ukraine funding within six months and cap France's EU contribution at EUR 5bn.

timeline.title: France's EU funding debate comes under scrutiny
timeline.detail: A JournalArta explainer says France's position on EU funding is under pressure; we know only the headline.

timeline.title: Parliament moves to protect Erasmus and research
timeline.detail: EU Perspectives reports that the European Parliament wants these programmes shielded in the next budget as debt bills mount.

timeline.title: Costa sets the next budget showdown
timeline.detail: A headline reports that the Council president has set the next confrontation on the budget; we have no further detail.

timeline.title: Austria threatens to block the budget
timeline.detail: Reports say Chancellor Stocker is considering a veto, which would make unanimity harder to reach.

timeline.title: Transport groups demand funding be kept
timeline.detail: Dozens of European organisations call for transport spending to be maintained in the 2028-2034 budget.

timeline.title: Deforestation rules start for large and medium operators
timeline.detail: The Green Deal rule whose enforcement the next budget funds; small firms follow on 30 June 2027.

timeline.title: Target date for a budget deal
timeline.detail: Leaders aim to settle before elections in France, Spain, Italy and Poland.

timeline.title: Carbon border certificates go on sale
timeline.detail: The first declaration is due 30 September 2027.

timeline.title: French presidential election, first round
timeline.detail: The run-off follows on 2 May 2027; the National Rally candidate leads October polls at 35-36%.

causes.name: Unanimity rule
causes.detail: The seven-year budget needs every member state in the Council, then Parliament's consent, so one government can hold it hostage.

causes.name: Rising debt repayment bills
causes.detail: The cost of past joint borrowing is squeezing room for new spending, according to EU Perspectives.

causes.name: New priorities competing with old programmes
causes.detail: A new Competitiveness Fund and defence and Ukraine needs compete with farm, regional and research lines, according to Elcano.

causes.name: Austria's veto threat
causes.detail: Reports that Chancellor Stocker is considering blocking the budget raised the stakes of unanimity.

causes.name: Macron's push for a 2026 deal
causes.detail: Paris wants agreement before a vote that could change France's position.

causes.name: The election calendar
causes.detail: France, Spain, Italy and Poland all vote around 2027. A Spanish snap election follows a planned November strike, and its date is not yet confirmed.

causes.name: Le Pen's lead and pledges
causes.detail: She polls at 35-36% and promises to cap France's EU contribution at EUR 5bn, end Ukraine funding within six months and stop the Green Deal.

causes.name: Lobbying surge
causes.detail: Parliament, transport groups and research bodies are all defending lines at once.

stakeholders.name: Emmanuel Macron
stakeholders.wants: A bigger budget agreed this year, before the French vote
stakeholders.leverage: France is a large net contributor and a key voice in the Council
stakeholders.likelyMove: Press leaders for a December deal and frame delay as a risk to Europe

stakeholders.name: Marine Le Pen and the National Rally
stakeholders.wants: France's net payment cut from about EUR 8bn to EUR 5bn, an end to Ukraine funding and a stop to the Green Deal
stakeholders.leverage: A 35-36% first-round poll lead; a threat to reopen any deal after the vote
stakeholders.likelyMove: Call the rush to agree a deal anti-democratic and make the budget a campaign issue

stakeholders.name: Austria and Chancellor Stocker
stakeholders.wants: Unknown; the reports do not say which terms Vienna is seeking
stakeholders.leverage: Each government can block a unanimous decision
stakeholders.likelyMove: Hold the veto threat as leverage and trade it for concessions

stakeholders.name: European Parliament
stakeholders.leverage: It can withhold consent from the final package
stakeholders.likelyMove: Defend its priority programmes against cuts as debt bills rise

stakeholders.name: Antonio Costa and the Commission
stakeholders.role: Brokers of a deal (European Council president; Commission led by von der Leyen)
stakeholders.wants: A settled budget on a short timetable
stakeholders.leverage: Control of the agenda and the negotiating text
stakeholders.likelyMove: Push leaders toward a package at or after the next summit; details not in our sources

stakeholders.name: Ukraine and Zelensky
stakeholders.leverage: Moral and political pressure; he has said lives are worth more than the price of aid
stakeholders.likelyMove: Lobby leaders for a protected Ukraine line in the budget

stakeholders.name: Transport and research lobbies
stakeholders.wants: Their lines kept in the 2028-2034 budget
stakeholders.leverage: Organised campaigns and ties to Parliament
stakeholders.likelyMove: Keep public pressure on until the numbers are fixed

sectors.why: Parliament is fighting to shield Erasmus and research money, but debt costs and competing priorities leave their final share open.
Lobbying is intense, yet transport funding can be squeezed by a new competitiveness logic.
EU channels carry much of the aid for Kyiv. A bigger budget helps, while Le Pen's pledge to end funding is a risk after the French vote.
New deforestation and carbon border rules mean paperwork and costs, and enforcement depends on budget money.
Rising debt repayment bills squeeze the budget; a large new package could mean more joint financing, though this is our general reading and we have no figures.
A new Competitiveness Fund is a central part of the proposed budget logic, according to Elcano.
Many competing campaigns raise demand for advocacy and consultancy work around the talks.

dailyLife.effect: Erasmus exchanges depend on the 2028-2034 budget; Parliament wants them protected.
Rail and other transport projects co-funded by the EU are lobbying to keep their funding.

dailyLife.item: Imports of coffee, wood, steel and aluminium
dailyLife.effect: New deforestation and carbon border rules add paperwork and costs for importers, which can reach prices over time.
France pays roughly EUR 8bn a year net to the EU; Le Pen wants EUR 5bn, which would shift costs to others or cut programmes.
How far Europe can keep funding Kyiv after 2027 depends partly on the EU budget.

scenarios.name: Talks slip into 2027
scenarios.looksLike: No deal at the December summit; leaders keep negotiating into the first half of 2027, with the French vote looming over every round.
signposts: Austria keeps its veto threat live into December
Costa and the Commission do not table a final package
Parliament publicly refuses a deal that cuts Erasmus and research
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Planning uncertainty for programmes and Ukraine support; the French campaign becomes partly about the budget.

scenarios.name: Deal by end of 2026
scenarios.looksLike: Leaders agree on a thinner or reshuffled package at the December summit, with concessions to the holdouts.
signposts: Austria's demands are met or dropped
A negotiating text circulates before December
scenarios.effectOnWorld: Macron's larger-budget position is locked in before the vote; Ukraine and Green Deal funding gain visibility.

scenarios.name: Veto standoff
scenarios.looksLike: One or more governments hold out into 2028; the EU relies on stopgap annual arrangements under the old ceilings once the current framework ends.
signposts: A formal veto is cast or declared
New governments harden positions after the 2027 elections
scenarios.effectOnWorld: New programmes start late, new priorities are underfunded and Ukraine's EU funding is less predictable.

scenarios.name: French rewrite
scenarios.looksLike: A deal is struck, but a National Rally victory in May 2027 leads Paris to demand a lower contribution and reopen it.
signposts: Le Pen wins the first round and leads polls for the run-off
Paris announces a EUR 5bn cap as a formal position
scenarios.effectOnWorld: The EU faces a budget fight over Ukraine, Green Deal funding and the size of the whole package.

predictions.text: Leaders will not agree a full 2028-2034 budget package at or before the end-2026 target. Probability about 70%.
Austria will formally state a veto or block a decision on the budget before any final agreement. Probability about 30%.
The final package will keep Erasmus and research as ring-fenced or named lines, with Parliament securing at least some protection. Probability about 60%.
The EU will not have a fully adopted 2028-2034 budget regulation by the end of the current framework. Probability about 35%.
The National Rally candidate will lead the first round on 18 April 2027, keeping the EU budget in the campaign. Probability about 65%.

actions: Plan for the deforestation rules from 30 December 2026 and carbon border certificates from 1 February 2027, whatever happens to the budget.
Do not assume EU grant lines will be settled before 2027; keep funding applications flexible.
Model scenarios where programmes start late in 2028.
Treat a year-end deal as possible but less likely than a slip into 2027.
Watch for a formal Austrian veto and for how France's positions move with polls.
Remember that a French election outcome could reopen any agreement.
Students and families relying on Erasmus should follow Parliament's line on the programme.
Expect no immediate change in daily life; budget effects arrive from 2028.
Watch for price effects on imported goods as new Green Deal rules take hold.
Separate Ukraine funding from the main budget fight, so it cannot be blocked by a single veto.
Set a clear negotiating text before the Spanish and French votes to reduce the room for rewrites.
Be open about what gets cut: debt repayment bills reduce what is left for new priorities.

analogues.whatFollowed: Leaders agreed in July after a marathon summit. Hungary and Poland then vetoed over the rule-of-law link, and a compromise came in December.
After long talks, the first agreed real-terms cut in an EU multiannual budget came in February 2013, after the Parliament pushed back on the details.
A June summit failed over the rebate and farm spending, and a deal was reached in December under a new presidency.

watch.title: December European Council
watch.why: The most likely venue for a deal or for a visible failure; exact date not yet confirmed in our material.

watch.title: Deforestation rules start for large and medium operators
watch.why: The first real test of Green Deal enforcement while the budget remains open.

watch.title: Carbon border certificate sales open
watch.why: Shows how the Green Deal machinery runs as the political fight continues.

watch.title: Spain's snap election date
watch.why: A new Spanish government could change its budget position; the date is not yet confirmed.

watch.title: Austria's formal position
watch.why: Whether the veto threat turns into a formal block, or into demands that can be met.

watch.title: French presidential election, first round
watch.why: The National Rally's result sets France's stance on the EU contribution, Ukraine and the Green Deal.

watch.title: French presidential run-off
watch.why: The final French decision; a deal reached before it can be reopened afterward.

evidence.method: Drafted from the listed sources, the matched wire headlines of 24 to 26 October 2026 and the event's connection notes. For most items we saw only headlines and short summaries, not full articles, so details such as Austria's demands and the Council's plan are unknown. The Commission's 2025 proposal and the unanimity and consent rules are from general knowledge. Probabilities, scenario weights and the likely moves of each stakeholder are the author's estimates.
